concepts.title: Electric Current, Potential Difference and Resistance
concepts.body: Electric current is the rate at which electric charge flows through a conductor, measured in amperes. Potential difference, or voltage, is the work done to move a unit charge between two points, measured in volts. Ohm's law states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided temperature stays constant. The constant of proportionality is the resistance, measured in ohms. Resistance depends on the material's resistivity, the conductor's length, its cross‑sectional area, and temperature; it does not depend on the magnitude of the current itself. Resistivity is a property of the material and has the unit ohm‑metre.

concepts.title: Combination of Resistors
concepts.body: When resistors are connected in series the same current passes through each, and the total resistance is the arithmetic sum of the individual resistances. In a parallel arrangement the voltage across each resistor is the same, while the total current splits among the branches; the reciprocal of the equivalent resistance equals the sum of the reciprocals of each resistance. Consequently the equivalent resistance of a parallel network is always smaller than the smallest individual resistor. Household wiring uses parallel connections so that each appliance receives the full supply voltage, whereas decorative light strings often use series connections.

concepts.title: Heating Effect and Electric Power
concepts.body: When current flows through a resistor, electrical energy is converted into heat; this Joule heating is given by H = I² R t. The rate at which energy is transferred is electric power, expressed as P = V I = I² R = V² / R. Common appliances such as electric heaters, toasters and kettles exploit the heating effect. Electrical energy consumed commercially is measured in kilowatt‑hours; 1 kWh equals 3.6 × 10⁶ joules.

formulas.title: Ohm's Law
formulas.body: V = I R (V in volt [V], I in ampere [A], R in ohm [Ω]) – V is the potential difference across the conductor, I is the current through it, and R is its resistance.

formulas.title: Electric Power
formulas.body: P = V I (P in watt [W], V in volt [V], I in ampere [A]) – P is the power dissipated or supplied, V the voltage across the device, and I the current through it. Equivalent forms are P = I² R and P = V² / R.

examples.title: Equivalent Resistance of Parallel Resistors
examples.body: Find the equivalent resistance of a 4 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor connected in parallel. 1/Req = 1/4 + 1/6 = (3 + 2)/12 = 5/12. Therefore Req = 12/5 = 2.4 Ω.

examples.title: Power and Energy in a Simple Circuit
examples.body: A 12 V battery supplies a steady current of 2 A to a resistor. Power dissipated: P = V I = 12 × 2 = 24 W. Energy consumed in 10 minutes (600 s): E = P × t = 24 × 600 = 14400 J. In kilowatt‑hours: 14400 J ÷ 3.6×10⁶ = 0.004 kWh.

mcqs.question: What is the SI unit of resistance?
mcqs.explanation: Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω), the SI unit named after Georg Ohm.

mcqs.question: Two resistors of 3 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel across a 12 V supply. What is the total current drawn from the supply?
mcqs.explanation: First find equivalent resistance: 1/Req = 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2 → Req = 2 Ω. Then total current I = V / Req = 12 V / 2 Ω = 6 A.

mcqs.question: An electric kettle rated 1500 W operates on 230 V. What is the resistance of its heating element?
mcqs.explanation: Use P = V² / R → R = V² / P = (230)² / 1500 = 52900 / 1500 ≈ 35.27 Ω, which rounds to 35.3 Ω.
